title: Oaths by time
hookLine: oaths by the dawn, the forenoon, the afternoon, the night: time as sacred

lines: THE BOOK SWEARS BY THE CLOCK.
cards: Check the clock right now. Whatever it says, the Qur'an has probably sworn by it. Early, before the sun: by the dawn.
Mid-morning, light at full strength: by the forenoon. Late afternoon, shadows long: by the declining day. After dark: by the night when it covers.
Four surahs are named for those hours. The book doesn't only mention time. It takes oaths by it, the way it swore by the pen, the wind and the stars.

teach.b: Here they are, in Pickthall's translation. Surah eighty-nine: "By the Dawn." Surah ninety-three: "By the morning hours."
Surah one hundred three: "By the declining day." Surah ninety-two: "By the night enshrouding." Al-Fajr, ad-Duha, al-'Asr, al-Layl.
An oath in Arabic sets something up as witness to what follows, and commentators say Allah swears by created things to draw attention to them. So the hours are held up as signs. Take the shortest.

teach.h: AL-'ASR: TIME, AND THE HUMAN IN LOSS.
teach.b: By time, or by the declining day, surely the human is in loss, except those who believe and do good and urge one another to truth and to patience. 'Asr means late afternoon, and also time itself, an age; commentators read it both ways.
Imam ash-Shafi'i is reported to have said that if people reflected on this surah alone, it would be enough for them. Then the daily prayers. Fajr, dawn.
Dhuhr, midday. 'Asr, afternoon. Maghrib, sunset. 'Isha', nightfall.
The names of the prayers are names of hours. Five times a day, the clock itself becomes the call. A hadith qudsi in al-Bukhari goes further.
Allah says: the son of Adam curses time, but I am time; in My hand is the command, and I turn the night and the day. In this book, time isn't what stands between you and what matters.
It's one of the things that matters, sworn by, and turning in Allah's hand.

how: Muslims pray five times a day at prayer times named for the hours (fajr, dhuhr, 'asr, maghrib, 'isha'); surah al-'Asr is short and often recited, and a report says two companions would not part until one had recited it to the other.

o: by the declining day, or by time itself
the midday prayer, when the sun is highest
a promise made before witnesses at dusk

games.q: oaths by time — tap the pairs.

s: the daily prayers are named for times of day
fajr, dhuhr, 'asr, maghrib, 'isha': dawn to nightfall.
it can also mean time itself, an age; commentators read 103:1 both ways.
a hadith qudsi warns against cursing time
in al-Bukhari: the son of Adam curses time, but I am time; I turn the night and the day.

games.q: surah al-'Asr says the human is in loss, except those who do four things. which is one of them?
games.why: believe, do good, urge one another to truth, and urge one another to patience.

practice: Without checking a clock, look around: where is the light coming from, and is it thin, full, slanting or gone?

Name the hour by its look, not its number, early, full morning, the long afternoon, dusk, deep night, and if you'd like, say that hour's oath once, quietly: by the dawn, by the morning hours, by the declining day, or by the night.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Asr. By the declining day, or by time itself: a three-verse surah Imam ash-Shafi'i said would be enough for people, if they reflected on it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 103:1: by the declining day, or by time.

carryVoice: Your line: by time. Every hour is a sign. Day six hundred eighty-five, and counting.

sources.ref: saying attributed to ash-Shafi'i on al-'Asr (cited in Ibn Kathir's tafsir)
